expected_utility: Read the Expected Utility card as a way to keep several possible worlds on the page at once. The formula is not claiming that an average world will happen; it is making a fair comparison before the hidden state is known. First list the states, then their chances, then the utility in each state. The Bayes Rule card is the companion move after evidence arrives: the weights on the possible worlds must be revised rather than reused.
extensive_form_games: Use the Backward Induction card to read a game tree as a machine for testing future credibility. A branch is not a promise that the player will take it; it is an option that must still be attractive when that node is reached. The math compresses each solved future choice into a value and passes that value backward. If the tree hides what a player observes, the calculation can look clean while solving the wrong situation.
dominance: The Dominance Inequality card is the exact test behind deleting a move. It says: compare two actions while holding each opponent contingency fixed, and do that for every contingency the model allows. The key word is every. A strategy that loses under one likely story is not dominated yet; it must fail across the full table. This is why dominance can prune before beliefs or equilibrium are solved.
iterated_deletion: The Dominance Inequality card gives the one-round deletion test; iterated deletion repeats the same test after earlier impossible moves have been removed. The mathematical idea is simple but powerful: once the game shrinks, some actions that previously looked possible may lose their support. Keep a deletion log, because the proof depends on what was known and removed at each round, not just on the final surviving list.
rationalizability: Use Expected Utility and Bayes Rule to understand rationalizability as a belief test, not a prediction test. The question is whether some coherent belief over the opponent's possible actions can make this action optimal. If yes, the action may survive even when it is not part of a Nash equilibrium. The math keeps the belief explicit so the analyst cannot dismiss an action merely because it looks strange under one favorite forecast.
best_response: The Best Response card turns the vague phrase 'smartest move' into a conditional calculation. Hold the other players' actions, beliefs, or type-contingent rules fixed; then compare the player's available actions under that fixed environment. The notation argmax just means 'keep the action with the largest payoff.' The trap is treating the result as globally best. It is only best against the thing you held fixed.
nash_equilibrium: The Nash card closes a loop made from best-response checks. Start with a proposed outcome, freeze everyone except one player, and ask whether that player wants to switch. Repeat for every player. The mathematical condition means each chosen action belongs to that player's best-response set. It does not mean the outcome is fair, efficient, or collectively desirable; it only means no single player has a profitable one-person escape.
mixed_strategies: Use Nash and Expected Utility together here. A mixed strategy is not a player being indecisive; it is a probability plan that can make the opponent unable to exploit a predictable pure action. The calculation usually asks which probability makes the other player indifferent between two actions. Indifference is the signal that neither pure action can be targeted. Always check whose payoff is being equalized, because it is easy to solve for the wrong player.
zero_sum_games: The Nash and Best Response cards show why zero-sum games have a special flavor. Each player is still making a local best-response calculation, but the payoff table has a fixed total, so one side's gain is exactly the other side's loss. Before using zero-sum reasoning, add the payoffs in each cell. If the total changes, the interaction may include shared gains, shared losses, or outside effects that break the pure-security logic.
minimax: The Best Response card gives the local comparison that minimax turns into a protective rule. Instead of asking what the opponent is likely to do, minimax asks what damage the opponent can force against each plan. The player then chooses the plan with the best worst case. This is a reasoning move for adversarial settings; if interests partly align or the opponent lacks information, worst-case logic may be too cautious.
backward_induction: The Backward Induction card is the procedure behind this concept. Start at the last real choices, solve what the moving player will want there, replace those future nodes with their values, and move one step earlier. The math matters because early threats and promises inherit their force from later incentives. If a future action is unattractive when the future arrives, it should not discipline the present unless the model adds reputation, commitment, or outside consequences.
subgame_perfection: Read this through Backward Induction and Nash together. Nash checks whether players want to deviate at the proposed outcome; subgame perfection asks that the same kind of credibility survive inside every proper continuation game. The math blocks empty threats by jumping to the place the threat would be tested. If information sets prevent a proper subgame, then beliefs rather than subgame structure may be carrying the prediction.
one_shot_deviation: The Backward Induction card explains why local future temptations matter. A one-shot deviation check changes only today's action at a particular history and then returns to the planned continuation. If no such local switch pays, the larger dynamic plan can be credible under the right technical conditions. The shortcut is dangerous when profitable deviations require several coordinated changes over time or when continuation values are not well defined.
bargaining: The Discounted Payoff Sum card explains why time changes bargaining power. Waiting transforms future gains into present value, so a formally larger future payoff can be less attractive than a smaller payoff now. In bargaining problems, separate total surplus from disagreement payoffs first, then use discounting to see how delay, patience, or outside options change the split. The math should not hide the basic question: who can afford to wait?
finitely_repeated_games: Use Backward Induction to read finite repetition. The known final round has no later round to punish cheating, so its answer can remove discipline from the next-to-last round, and so on. The calculation walks backward because each earlier period depends on what future punishment remains. If the ending is uncertain, reputation continues outside the model, or punishment can happen elsewhere, the simple unraveling logic may no longer apply.
infinitely_repeated_games: The Discounted Payoff Sum card is the mathematical pressure behind repeated cooperation. The comparison is between a one-period temptation and the present value of future punishment or lost cooperation. Infinite time does not automatically create discipline; the future must be valuable enough, cheating must be observed well enough, and punishment must be credible. Read the powers of delta as the shrinking weight of consequences farther from today.
folk_theorem: Use the Discounted Payoff Sum and Nash cards together. The folk theorem says many feasible payoff patterns can be supported when future discipline is strong enough, but each candidate still needs a no-deviation check. The math is not a prediction machine saying what will happen. It is a supportability test: can promised rewards and punishments make today's restraint privately worthwhile for every player?
implicit_cartels: The Discounted Payoff Sum card explains how high prices can be sustained without a written contract. A firm compares the gain from undercutting today with the discounted stream of losses from future price wars or retaliation. The equation forces the story to name monitoring and punishment rather than simply saying 'future matters.' The auction payment card becomes relevant only when a market rule also shapes expected payments or allocation incentives.
imperfect_competition: The Best Response card shows why a firm with market power cannot solve its problem as if rivals were scenery. Profit depends on the firm's own price or quantity and on rivals' choices, so each firm has a response curve rather than a standalone optimum. The market prediction comes from response curves fitting together. If entry, capacity, product differences, or repeated interaction matter, the two-firm calculation is only a first pass.
bayesian_games: Expected Utility and Bayes Rule are the two math moves behind Bayesian games. Expected utility lets a player choose while rival types are still hidden. Bayes rule explains how beliefs should move when signals or actions are observed. The important modeling step is to make strategies type-contingent: each private type needs its own action rule. Replacing hidden information with one average opponent usually erases the strategic problem.
types_and_beliefs: Bayes Rule explains how observations revise probabilities over hidden types, while Expected Utility explains how those probabilities guide action before the type is known. A type is not a personality label; it is a hidden fact that changes payoffs, feasible actions, or information. The math matters because it separates the hidden fact from the belief about that fact. If no observation can move the belief, say so explicitly.
bayesian_nash_equilibrium: Expected Utility gives the payoff comparison under hidden information, Best Response gives the conditional choice test, and Nash closes the loop across all types. A Bayesian Nash equilibrium is not one action per player; it is a strategy rule for each type. To audit it, hold other type-contingent rules fixed and check whether each type wants to deviate. An average incentive check can hide a failing type.
screening_and_adverse_selection: Bayes Rule explains how observed choices reveal hidden types, while Expected Utility explains why those types choose before revelation. The math is about composition: a price or contract does not just change revenue per participant, it can change who participates. After any rule change, recompute the pool. The auction expected-payment card is a related design move: rules can make private information strategically visible or keep it hidden.
auctions: The Auction Expected Payment card separates three pieces that are easy to blur: bid, chance of winning, and payment if winning. Expected Utility then adds the bidder's value from winning, while Bayes Rule explains how beliefs over rival values enter the chance of winning. A higher bid can help and hurt at the same time. Always read the payment rule before importing intuition from another auction format.
revenue_equivalence: The Auction Expected Payment card is the entry point because revenue equivalence is about expected payment patterns, not surface similarity between auction rules. First-price and second-price auctions can induce different bids while producing the same expected revenue under tight assumptions. The mathematical audit is a checklist: same allocation rule, same lowest-type payoff, risk neutrality, independent private values, symmetry, and no changed entry or reserve structure.
ad_auctions: The Auction Expected Payment card explains why platform auctions are not just rank lists. A bid affects allocation chances and payment, while quality scores and click probabilities change what a slot is worth. Separate bid, predicted click behavior, ranking, and payment before doing the incentive story. Otherwise a single platform score can hide three different mechanisms: who gets shown, what users do, and what advertisers pay.
perfect_bayesian_equilibrium: Bayes Rule explains belief updating after observed play, Backward Induction explains sequential credibility, and Expected Utility explains optimal action under those beliefs. PBE requires strategies and beliefs to fit together. On the path, beliefs should follow from Bayes rule. Off the path, extra belief assumptions may be needed, and those assumptions can drive the result. Do not let the notation make off-path discipline look automatic.
signaling: Bayes Rule explains how a receiver reads a signal as evidence about hidden type, while Expected Utility explains why a sender chooses the signal only if it is worth the cost. The key mathematical question is whether different types have different incentives to imitate. If both types want the same visible action, the signal pools and reveals little. If imitation is too costly for one type, separation can occur.
cheap_talk: Bayes Rule explains how messages could move beliefs, but Expected Utility and incentive reasoning explain why words may fail. Because cheap-talk messages cost nothing directly, the receiver must ask why different sender types would choose different messages. If all types prefer the same persuasive claim, hearing it conveys little. Communication becomes informative only when preferences are aligned enough, or structured enough, that messages are strategically credible.
common_knowledge: The Common Knowledge Recursion card shows why coordination can require more than everyone knowing the same fact. The sequence E, KE, KKE, and so on is a ladder of publicness: the fact, everyone knowing the fact, everyone knowing that everyone knows, and so forth. The math matters when action depends on confidence about others' confidence. Private notice can spread information without creating the shared basis for coordinated behavior.
